channel.title: Soft Home Global — working notes
channel.description: Denial code guides, accounts receivable, prior authorization, eligibility and Davis-Bacon certified payroll. Written for people with the problem open in front of them.

item.title: Days in AR: how to calculate it, and the number it hides
item.description: Four divisions give the figures every outside party asks for. Why most practices cannot produce them on the day, and which one matters.

item.title: What must be on a Good Faith Estimate, and when it has to be issued
item.description: Every element 45 CFR 149.610 requires, the four notices most templates leave out, and the three deadlines that govern it.

item.title: What a denied claim actually costs to work, and what it costs to ignore
item.description: Two published figures decide it: what a rework costs, and how much of a denied claim is eventually paid when worked. Both are checkable.

item.title: How long can a payer take to decide a prior authorization?
item.description: Since 1 January 2026 there is a federal answer: 72 hours expedited, seven calendar days standard. Which payers it reaches, and which it does not.

item.title: How to write an appeal letter that actually gets a claim reopened
item.description: Most appeals ask the payer to please review the claim, and most are denied twice. The four parts that change that, and where each comes from.

item.title: A worked example: ninety days of aged AR, taken apart
item.description: Not a client. Invented numbers, shown as invented, worked the way we would actually work them — because we would rather show the method than claim a result.

item.title: Medicaid filing limits: 21 states publish one, 30 do not
item.description: We tried to source all 51 from the regulation. Twenty-one we could quote, thirty we could not, and that gap is the finding. With the method.

item.title: Modifier 26 and TC: who bills which half
item.description: A diagnostic service can be two claims or one, and billing the wrong half is one of the quietest ways to lose money in radiology and cardiology.

item.title: The 8-minute rule, and the units it costs you
item.description: Timed codes are billed on total treatment time, not per code, and the two ways of counting produce different answers on the same visit.

item.title: How long payer enrollment actually takes
item.description: The honest ranges, what makes each one longer, and the dates that quietly deactivate a provider who is already enrolled.

item.title: How to read an 835 remittance without missing money
item.description: The single highest-value skill on a billing floor. Six fields decide whether a balance is yours to chase, the patient’s to pay, or nobody’s.

item.title: Seven things that trigger a certified payroll audit
item.description: Reviewers look at a small number of things first. Each one is visible without reading a single wage rate, and each one is avoidable.

item.title: Form WH-347, box by box
item.description: The federal certified payroll form, field by field, and the four boxes that account for most rejections.

item.title: Why prior authorizations get delayed, and how to stop it
item.description: Almost every authorization delay traces to one of eight causes, and six of them are inside the practice rather than at the payer.

item.title: What a good clean claim rate actually is
item.description: The number quoted everywhere is 95%. It is close to meaningless without a definition, and the definition is where practices and vendors quietly disagree.

item.title: How to overturn a timely filing denial
item.description: A timely filing denial is not always final, and the thing that overturns it is almost never an argument. It is a record showing the claim arrived on time.

item.title: How certified payroll filing works, week by week
item.description: Certified payroll is a weekly deadline that never moves, on projects with different rules each. This is what a dedicated seat does, and what a contractor has to define first.

item.title: How chronic care management and RPM billing work
item.description: These programmes are administratively heavy and clinically light, which is why they stall. This is what the administrative layer has to do for the clinical work to be billable.

item.title: How dental billing and medical cross-coding work
item.description: Dental plans limit what they pay in ways medical plans do not — annual maximums, frequency limits, waiting periods, missing tooth clauses. Verification here is a treatment-planning input, not a formality.

item.title: How DME billing works, and why documentation decides it
item.description: In durable medical equipment the claim is the easy part. The documentation file behind it decides whether the claim survives, and it has to be complete before the item ships.

item.title: How behavioural health and ABA billing work
item.description: This is authorization-unit accounting as much as billing. Run out of approved units mid-course and the sessions still happen — they just stop being billable.

item.title: How workers’ compensation billing differs from commercial
item.description: These claims pay slowly, on different rules, to a different party, and they need a queue that is not the commercial one. This is what that queue has to contain.

item.title: How to find payer underpayments nobody is looking for
item.description: A denial announces itself. An underpayment does not — it looks exactly like a payment. This is how to build the comparison that finds them and the evidence that recovers them.

item.title: How release of information works, and the 30-day clock
item.description: Records requests are a queue with legal deadlines attached, handled in most practices by whoever has a spare afternoon. This is how to run it as a tracked function with an audit trail that survives being asked about.

item.title: How hospital patient access and pre-registration work
item.description: Registration is where most denials are created and where almost none are detected. This is what pre-registration and financial clearance should cover, and how to staff it as a defined queue.

item.title: What a virtual medical assistant actually does
item.description: A virtual medical assistant works if the role is scoped as a defined set of queues and fails if it is scoped as "help". This is the difference, in practical terms, and what to decide before the first day.

item.title: How referral intake and coordination work
item.description: A referral that arrives by fax and is never logged is a patient the practice never sees and a referrer who stops sending. This is how to run intake so every referral is tracked from arrival to booked visit.

item.title: How scheduling, recall and no-show recovery work
item.description: An empty slot is not recoverable — the hour passes whether or not somebody is in it. This is how a dedicated seat fills the template, works the recall list, and gets cancellations back on the books the same day.

item.title: How patient billing and statements work
item.description: Patient balances are the part of accounts receivable most likely to be billed wrongly and least likely to be chased consistently. This is how to run the cycle without damaging the relationship the practice depends on.

item.title: How provider credentialing works, and what stalls it
item.description: Credentialing is administratively simple and operationally brutal, because everything depends on dates nobody is watching. This is how to staff the chase and keep a calendar that prevents the expensive version.

item.title: How medical coding works in a practice
item.description: Coding is the one back-office function where being fast and wrong is worse than being slow. This is how to set up an outsourced coding seat so the record leads and the query process actually works.

item.title: How charge entry and claim submission work
item.description: Charge lag is the cheapest problem in the revenue cycle to fix and the least often measured. This is how a dedicated charge entry seat runs, what it should scrub before submission, and what has to be decided first.

item.title: How payment posting works, and where money hides
item.description: Payment posting decides what every other report in the practice says. Posted carelessly, it hides denials inside adjustments and makes the ageing report fiction. This is how to run it properly.

item.title: How denial management works, and what it costs to skip
item.description: Reworking denials one at a time is labour. Classifying them is the part that stops next month’s. This is how to run a denial queue that does both, and what to define before handing it to anybody.

item.title: How prior authorization works, start to finish
item.description: Authorization work fails in the gap between submitting and deciding. This is how to staff the chase, what to record, and how to stop authorizations expiring quietly before the service is rendered.

item.title: How eligibility verification actually works
item.description: Most of what a practice loses to coverage problems is decided before the patient arrives. This is what a dedicated eligibility seat checks, when it checks it, and how to set the queue up so the front desk stops finding out at the counter.

item.title: What breaks at two, five and ten providers
item.description: Billing does not degrade smoothly as a practice grows. It breaks at predictable sizes, and each break has a different fix.

item.title: Seven signs your billing company is underperforming
item.description: Most practices find out late, because the reporting they receive is designed to look reassuring. What to ask for, and what the answers should be.

item.title: Days in AR: what the number hides and how to move it
item.description: A single average conceals the accounts that are actually costing you. The three cuts of the same data that tell you where the labour should go.

item.title: Switching billing companies without losing a month of revenue
item.description: The handover is where the money is lost — in the claims in flight and the ageing report nobody agreed to own. A sequence that protects both.

item.title: In-house biller or outsourced? An honest decision framework
item.description: When hiring locally is genuinely right, when it is not, and the cost comparison that uses what an employer actually pays rather than the salary line.

item.title: Why insurers deny claims, and which denials are worth fighting
item.description: Most denials are recoverable and most are never worked. The published data on denial rates, what it costs to fight one, and how to decide which to chase.

item.title: How much should medical billing cost? The published numbers
item.description: Percentage of collections, per claim, flat monthly, or a salary. What each one actually costs a practice, with the figures the vendors themselves publish.

item.title: Volume is the same but the deposit is smaller. Where did it go?
item.description: Same schedule, same providers, smaller cheque. There are five places the money goes, and three reports you already have will tell you which one.

item.title: N290: Missing, incomplete or invalid rendering provider identifier
item.description: The NPI of the clinician who performed the service is missing from the claim, is not a valid NPI, or is not one the payer has linked to your group.

item.title: N4: Missing or invalid primary payer explanation of benefits
item.description: The secondary payer will not adjudicate without the primary payer’s decision: what was allowed, paid and adjusted, line by line.

item.title: M51: Missing, incomplete or invalid procedure code
item.description: The code on the line is not one the payer recognises for that date: deleted, mistyped, or from the wrong code set.

item.title: MA27: Missing, incomplete or invalid Medicare number or name
item.description: Medicare cannot match the beneficiary: the Medicare Beneficiary Identifier or the name on the claim does not agree with the entitlement record.

item.title: M115: Denied — not a contract supplier for this item
item.description: A DMEPOS competitive bidding denial: for this item, in this area, Medicare pays only suppliers holding a contract, and this claim came from one that does not.

item.title: N830: Processed under surprise-billing rules — the patient cannot be balance billed
item.description: An out-of-network service the payer processed under federal or state surprise-billing rules: the patient owes only the PR amount, and any dispute over the payment is with the payer, not the patient.

item.title: MA30: Missing, incomplete or invalid type of bill
item.description: A facility claim problem: the three-digit type of bill in field 4 of the UB-04 does not fit the facility, the claim, or the frequency.

item.title: N522: Duplicate of a crossover claim
item.description: The secondary payer already has this claim — Medicare forwarded it automatically — and the copy you sent is the duplicate.

item.title: N381: Adjusted per the contract — read the contract
item.description: An alert, not a denial: the payer processed the line under your contract and is pointing you at it. The reason code beside it carries the money.

item.title: N362: Units of service exceed the payer’s maximum
item.description: The line carries more units than the payer allows for that code on one date, so it rejected the quantity rather than the service.

item.title: N122: Add-on code cannot be billed by itself
item.description: The code billed only exists alongside a primary procedure, and no acceptable primary was on the claim.

item.title: N115: Decision based on a Local Coverage Determination
item.description: A published coverage policy for your region decided this, and that policy states exactly what would have been covered.

item.title: N54: Claim inconsistent with the authorized services
item.description: There is an authorization, and what was billed does not match what it covers.

item.title: N34: Incorrect claim form or format for this service
item.description: The service was billed on the wrong form or in the wrong format for the payer.

item.title: N30: Patient ineligible for this service
item.description: The patient does not qualify for this particular service under their plan, even though they may hold coverage.

item.title: N29: Missing documentation, orders, notes or report
item.description: The payer needs clinical documentation it does not have.

item.title: MA130: Claim unprocessable — no appeal rights
item.description: The claim was rejected as unprocessable rather than denied. There is nothing to appeal — it has to be corrected and sent again as a new claim.

item.title: N382: Missing, incomplete or invalid patient identifier
item.description: The payer cannot match the patient from what was sent.

item.title: N130: Consult plan benefit documents for restrictions
item.description: The payer is pointing you at the plan document: there is a restriction on this service and the document says what it is.

item.title: CO-273: Coverage or program guidelines exceeded
item.description: The service is covered, but this instance went past a programme limit: more visits, units or sessions than the guideline allows.

item.title: CO-B10: Allowed amount reduced — a component of the procedure was already paid
item.description: The payer paid part of this procedure on another line or claim and has reduced this one to the difference, so the practice is not paid twice for the same work.

item.title: CO-272: Coverage or program guidelines not met
item.description: The service is covered in principle but this instance did not meet the programme’s conditions.

item.title: CO-256: Service not payable under the managed care contract
item.description: The managed care contract in force does not provide for payment of this service.

item.title: CO-253: Sequestration reduction in federal payment
item.description: A statutory percentage reduction applied to a federal payment. It is not a denial and there is nothing to appeal.

item.title: CO-251: Attachment or documentation incomplete or deficient
item.description: Something was sent, and it did not contain what the payer needed.

item.title: CO-242: Services not provided by network providers
item.description: The plan pays only for its own network, and this provider was not in it for this service.

item.title: CO-227: Requested information from the patient not supplied
item.description: The payer asked the patient for something — very often about other insurance or an accident — and did not get it.

item.title: CO-226: Requested information from the provider not supplied
item.description: The payer asked you for something, and either nothing arrived or what arrived did not answer the question.

item.title: CO-184: Ordering provider not eligible to order or prescribe
item.description: The provider named as ordering the service is not accepted by the payer in that role.

item.title: CO-183: Referring provider not eligible to refer
item.description: Somebody is named as the referring provider who the payer will not accept in that role.

item.title: CO-182: Procedure modifier invalid on the date of service
item.description: The modifier attached to the code was not valid on the day of the service.

item.title: CO-181: Procedure code invalid on the date of service
item.description: The code existed at some point but was not valid on the day the service happened.

item.title: CO-177: Patient has not met eligibility requirements
item.description: There is coverage, but the patient has not satisfied a condition the plan attaches to it.

item.title: CO-167: Diagnosis is not covered
item.description: The payer does not cover the condition you billed, whatever the procedure was.

item.title: CO-150: Information does not support this level of service
item.description: The payer accepts the visit happened but not at the level you billed — usually an E/M downcode.

item.title: CO-136: Failure to follow the prior payer’s coverage rules
item.description: This is a secondary claim, and the secondary payer says the primary’s rules were not followed before it reached them.

item.title: CO-39: Services denied at the time authorization was requested
item.description: The authorization was asked for and refused, and the service was delivered anyway.

item.title: CO-35: Lifetime benefit maximum reached
item.description: The policy has a lifetime cap on this benefit and the patient has used it.

item.title: CO-33: Insured has no dependent coverage
item.description: The subscriber’s policy covers the subscriber only, so a dependent’s claim has nothing to pay against.

item.title: CO-32: Patient is not an eligible dependent
item.description: The payer does not recognize this patient as a covered dependent on the subscriber’s policy.

item.title: CO-24: Charges covered under a capitation agreement
item.description: The payer says this service is included in a capitated arrangement, so there is no separate fee-for-service payment.

item.title: CO-15: Authorization number missing or invalid
item.description: There is an authorization requirement here, and the number you sent is absent, wrong, or does not cover what was billed.

item.title: CO-10: Diagnosis inconsistent with patient gender
item.description: The diagnosis code is one the payer only accepts for a different gender marker than the one on the claim.

item.title: CO-9: Diagnosis inconsistent with patient age
item.description: The diagnosis code you sent is one the payer only accepts for a different age group.

item.title: CO-5: Procedure inconsistent with place of service
item.description: The code you billed is not one the payer accepts for the setting the service happened in.

item.title: PR-1: Deductible amount
item.description: The payer applied this amount to the patient’s deductible. It is not a denial — it is the plan working as designed, and the balance is the patient’s.

item.title: CO-286: Appeal time limits not met
item.description: The appeal arrived after the payer’s deadline. The clock for appealing is separate from, and usually shorter than, the clock for filing.

item.title: PR-31: Patient cannot be identified as our insured
item.description: The payer cannot match the patient to a member record. Usually a demographic or identifier mismatch rather than a coverage lapse.

item.title: CO-107: Related or qualifying claim not identified
item.description: This service only pays when it is linked to another one, and the link is missing from the claim.

item.title: CO-231: Mutually exclusive procedures
item.description: The two procedures billed cannot clinically or by rule both have happened at the same encounter.

item.title: CO-236: Procedure/modifier combination not compatible
item.description: Two things billed on the same day conflict under NCCI edits or a state fee schedule. The pair is the problem, not either code alone.

item.title: CO-8: Procedure inconsistent with provider type
item.description: The payer does not expect a provider of this specialty to bill this code, based on the taxonomy attached to the claim.

item.title: CO-185: Rendering provider not eligible
item.description: The payer does not accept this provider as eligible for this service — an enrollment, credentialing or scope-of-practice problem rather than a coding one.

item.title: OA-23: Prior payer’s adjudication
item.description: This is a coordination of benefits adjustment on a secondary claim. It reflects what the primary payer already did rather than a problem with your claim.

item.title: PR-204: Not covered under the patient’s current plan
item.description: The service itself is excluded from this particular plan. This is a benefit design decision, not a coding error.

item.title: CO-288: Referral absent
item.description: The plan required a referral from the patient’s primary care physician and there is not one on file for this visit.

item.title: CO-198: Prior authorization exceeded
item.description: An authorization exists. The problem is that you went past what it allowed — more units, more visits, or a longer date range than was approved.

item.title: CO-252: Additional documentation required
item.description: The payer will not decide until it sees paperwork. Nothing happens until it arrives.

item.title: CO-234: Procedure not paid separately
item.description: The payer treats this service as part of another one, similar to CO-97 but usually driven by the fee schedule rather than an NCCI edit.

item.title: CO-170: Payment denied for this provider type
item.description: The service may be covered, but not when delivered or billed by a provider of this type.

item.title: CO-140: Patient identification number and name do not match
item.description: The member ID and the name on the claim disagree with the payer’s record.

item.title: CO-119: Benefit maximum reached
item.description: The patient has used up what the plan allows for this benefit in this period.

item.title: CO-96: Non-covered charges
item.description: The plan does not cover this service at all. Distinct from medical necessity, which is an argument about evidence.

item.title: CO-11: Diagnosis inconsistent with the procedure
item.description: The payer does not accept that the diagnosis submitted justifies the procedure performed.

item.title: CO-4: Procedure code inconsistent with the modifier
item.description: The code and the modifier disagree, or a modifier the payer required was not there.

item.title: CO-B7: Provider not certified or eligible on this date
item.description: A credentialing or enrollment problem rather than a claim problem: nothing this provider bills to this payer will pay until it is fixed, and it is rarely one claim.

item.title: CO-109: Not covered by this payer or contractor
item.description: It went to the wrong place.

item.title: CO-151: Information does not support this many services
item.description: The payer accepts the service but not the quantity or the frequency at which it was billed.

item.title: CO-27: Expenses incurred after coverage terminated
item.description: The patient was not covered on the date of service.

item.title: CO-22: May be covered by another payer
item.description: The payer thinks somebody else is primary. Until coordination of benefits is corrected on their file, nothing on this claim will pay.

item.title: CO-18: Exact duplicate claim or service
item.description: The payer already has this claim. Usually harmless, occasionally a sign that the original is stuck.

item.title: CO-97: Included in the payment for another service
item.description: The payer is bundling this code into another one on the same claim. Sometimes that is correct and sometimes it is not.

item.title: CO-45: Charge exceeds the fee schedule
item.description: A contractual write-off rather than a denial. It only becomes a problem when the allowed amount is wrong.

item.title: CO-50: Not deemed medically necessary
item.description: The payer does not accept that the documentation supports the service. This is a clinical argument, not a clerical one.

item.title: CO-29: Time limit for filing has expired
item.description: The claim arrived after the payer’s filing deadline. This one is usually terminal, which is why it deserves attention before it happens rather than after.

item.title: CO-16: Claim lacks information or has a submission error
item.description: Something on the claim is missing or malformed. On its own the code tells you nothing — the detail is in the remark code that comes with it.

item.title: CO-197: Prior authorization absent
item.description: The payer required prior authorization for this service and cannot find one attached to the claim.

item.title: What to actually ask about offshore data security
item.description: HIPAA does not prohibit offshore work. What it requires is specific, and most vendor security pages answer a different question.

item.title: Fringe benefits on certified payroll, explained properly
item.description: In our experience the second most common rejection, and the one that turns into a back-wage finding rather than a bounced filing.

item.title: What a missed revalidation actually costs
item.description: It is never one claim. A lapsed enrollment stops payment on everything behind it, and the recovery window is measured in weeks.

item.title: Days in AR: what good actually looks like
item.description: The benchmark everyone quotes is 30 to 40 days. That number is useless on its own, and this explains what to measure instead.

item.title: The eligibility checks that pay for themselves
item.description: Verifying at registration instead of at every visit is the cheapest mistake in a practice. Three denial codes explain why.

item.title: Twelve questions to ask any offshore billing vendor
item.description: Including the four we would find awkward. A vendor that cannot answer these plainly is telling you something.

item.title: The five reasons certified payroll comes back rejected
item.description: In order of how often we see them in public filing data, and why the fifth is the one that holds up a progress payment.

item.title: The prior authorization checklist that prevents CO-197
item.description: CO-197 is the most preventable denial in medicine. Six checks before the visit stop almost all of them, and each takes under a minute.

item.title: Why claims sit at 90 days, and what actually moves them
item.description: A balance passes 90 days for one of four reasons, and only one is the payer’s fault. How to tell them apart before spending labour on the wrong pile.
